title.title: Nonexpansive maps on reflexive spaces have fixed points
title.subtitle: Claim: in any real reflexive Banach space, a nonexpansive map of a closed bounded convex set fixes a point

plain: Stir a bowl without ever pulling two points apart: must some point stay put? Here, in any reflexive space

beats.text: Schematic: rotating a disk $C$ moves no two points further apart. It is nonexpansive
Iterating need not converge; the orbit can circle forever
Kirk asked: does reflexivity alone guarantee a fixed point? Claim: yes

steps: Take a smallest invariant set with no fixed point
Build a tree of averages of nearly fixed points
Along one branch a vector appears that weak compactness forbids

data.assume: a smallest set, no fixed point

achievement.label: Kirk's problem (1965)
statement: X \text{ reflexive},\ \ F: C \to C,\ \ \|Fa - Fb\| \le \|a - b\|
achievement.context: Before: uniformly convex spaces (Browder, Göhde, 1965) and normal structure (Kirk, 1965)
achievement.note: Earlier claimed proofs (2019, 2021) were not accepted; this one rests on Lean

verify.detail: The Lean statement is exactly the problem: closed bounded convex $C$, 1-Lipschitz $F$
verify.ourCheck: We read the Lean statement line by line; we did not build it

voice.text: Rotating a disk moves no two points apart. Does reflexivity alone guarantee a fixed point?
A smallest bad set yields a tree whose branch breaks compactness.
Claimed: yes, in every reflexive Banach space.

sources.quote: Browder and Göhde proved it for uniformly convex spaces in 1965, and Kirk under normal structure the same year.
Hanebaly published claimed proofs in 2019 and 2021 that were not accepted
In every real reflexive Banach space, every nonexpansive self-map of a nonempty closed bounded convex set has a fixed point. The Lean statement is exactly the problem:
Given the history of failed claims, the Lean check is what this one stands on.
C nonempty closed bounded convex, F: C->C 1-Lipschitz => fixed point
